summary: Games companies sell through pay-what-you-want tiers, bonus-laden virtual currency, and gifts that move across products. They also give away whole products free to build a habit, and they let buyers undo the purchase cheaply. Many of these offers reset on a schedule, so a customer who has already used one can be offered it again.

patterns.name: Beat-the-average tiers
patterns.how: The buyer picks the price, but the best items unlock only above the running average or at a fixed top tier. The average acts as a visible benchmark, so many people pay more than the $1 minimum to avoid getting the weaker set.
patterns.example: Humble Bundle sells games in tiers: a minimum-price tier, a tier that requires beating the average price, and a top fixed-price tier that unlocks everything.

patterns.name: Buyer-controlled payment split
patterns.how: At checkout the buyer decides how much of the payment goes to the creators, to charity, or to the platform. Choosing where the money goes makes the purchase feel like a good deed and not only a bargain.
patterns.example: Humble Bundle checkout has a slider that splits the payment between developers, charities and the platform. One review notes the slider's default charity share is set low.

patterns.name: Free-to-keep weekly giveaway
patterns.how: A store gives away complete games each week, and the buyer keeps them once claimed. This gets people to open the store on a schedule, builds their library on the platform, and puts paid items next to the free ones.
patterns.example: The Epic Games Store runs weekly free games, and its May 2026 Mega Sale paired them with discounts of up to 75% off.

patterns.name: Cross-product gift with purchase
patterns.how: Buying one product unlocks a cosmetic item in a different product the buyer may already love. It adds value without cutting the price, and it pulls players of the other product toward the purchase.
patterns.example: During the 2026 Epic Mega Sale, buying Super Meat Boy 3D gets you a Super Meat Boy Sidekick in Fortnite as a gift with purchase.

patterns.name: Store-wide cashback credit
patterns.how: A percentage of each purchase comes back as store credit that can only be spent in the same store. The buyer feels they are saving, and the credit is a reason to return and spend again.
patterns.example: In 2025 Epic boosted Epic Rewards to 20% back at checkout during its Mega Sale, and keeps 20% back permanently on in-game purchases in Fortnite, Rocket League and Fall Guys. The boost was extended to Jan 8, 2026, so check it is still running.

patterns.name: Playtime-based refund guarantee
patterns.how: The buyer can get a refund if they have played under a set number of hours within a set number of days. Because the promise is tied to actual use, buying feels safe, and it still limits abuse.
patterns.example: Steam refunds any game played for under two hours within 14 days of purchase. A recent change counts early-access hours toward that limit.

patterns.name: Resetting first-purchase doubler
patterns.how: The first purchase of each currency pack size gives double the currency, and the bonus resets on a schedule, such as an anniversary. This pushes buyers to try every pack size once, and lapsed spenders get a new reason to buy.
patterns.example: Genshin Impact doubles the Genesis Crystals on a player's first purchase of each tier, and it announced a full reset of this bonus for its 6th anniversary after the 7.1 update.

patterns.name: Bonus-currency price ladder
patterns.how: Currency packs are priced so that bigger packs carry a much larger bonus, while the smallest pack has no bonus. In-game items are then priced in that currency, so the real cost is harder to compare, and buyers are nudged toward bigger packs.
patterns.example: Genshin Impact's crystal packs run from 60 crystals at $0.99 up to 6480 plus a 1600 bonus at the top tier. The Welkin Moon pass is sold alongside at $4.99.
